title: During Wind and Rain: occasion
short: A poem of Hardy's later years, usually read in the light of his first wife Emma (died 27 November 1912) and published in Moments of Vision (1917).
body: Emma Lavinia Gifford, whom Hardy met in Cornwall in 1870, died at Max Gate in November 1912 after years of estrangement. Among her papers Hardy found a manuscript memoir of her early life, later published as Some Recollections. The four scenes of this poem, a family singing, gardening, breakfasting out of doors and moving house, are often read as images of the Gifford household in Emma's girlhood in Plymouth, a world Hardy never saw and knew only through her words; the link to her recollections is an interpretation, not something Hardy states. Dennis Taylor's 1975 article is a detailed study of the poem and of how it fits Hardy's poetic development. The poem is therefore an elegy at two removes: for Emma, and for the vanished family life she remembered. It was collected in Moments of Vision and Miscellaneous Verses (1917).

title: Title: 'wind and rain'
short: The title may recall the refrain of Feste's closing song in Twelfth Night, 'With hey, ho, the wind and the rain'.
body: Feste's song at the end of Twelfth Night moves a single life through its stages, from 'a little tiny boy' to age, against a refrain of weather that never changes: 'For the rain it raineth every day'. Hardy's title sets each of his happy scenes against the same steady weather of time, and the rain returns in the poem's last line to wear away the carved names. Hardy is not known to have pointed to the echo himself, so it is best treated as a suggestion; but the shared pattern of a song, a refrain and the passing years makes it apt. The word 'During' also matters: the scenes do not come before the storm but are lived inside it.

title: Treble, tenor and bass
short: The family sings in parts around an instrument, a domestic music-making Hardy knew from his own musical family.
body: Treble, tenor and bass are the voice parts of part-song or hymn singing; with 'one to play' (l. 4), presumably at the piano, the scene is a Victorian family evening. Hardy's father and grandfather had been church musicians at Stinsford, and music recurs in his poems as the sign of shared, now lost, community. The list form ('He, she, all of them', 'Treble and tenor and bass') makes the household a harmonious whole, and the same device returns in each stanza ('Elders and juniors', 'Men and maidens', 'Clocks and carpets and chairs'), so that the catalogue of people becomes a catalogue of things by the end.

title: yea / aye
short: Archaic affirmatives used as emphatic fillers, alternating 'yea' and 'aye' from stanza to stanza.
body: 'Yea' (yes, indeed) and 'aye' (yes) are old affirmative words; here they work less as meaning than as song-like intensifiers, completing the second line of each stanza in the manner of a ballad or carol. Their regular alternation (yea, aye, yea, aye) mirrors the alternation of the two refrains ('the years O!' and 'the years, the years'). 'Aye' can also be heard in its old sense of 'always', a quiet irony in a poem about how nothing lasts. The OED records both as emphatic affirmative words.

title: mooning
short: Hardy makes 'moon' a verb: the candlelight gives each face the pale round glow of a moon.
body: The verb is characteristic of Hardy's habit of coining or reviving compact words. The candles 'moon' the singers' faces, lighting them so that each looks pale, round and luminous like a small moon. The image is tender, but moons wane and candles burn down; the light that makes the faces beautiful already measures time. The ellipsis that follows (' . . .') marks the point at which the remembered scene breaks off and the speaker's present intrudes. The verb is unusual in this transferred sense, giving the line a striking compression.

title: Refrain: 'Ah, no; the years O!'
short: A broken refrain interrupts each happy scene, alternating between 'the years O!' and 'the years, the years'.
body: Each stanza builds a scene in the present tense and then is cut off by an ellipsis and a sigh. The refrain alternates between 'the years O!' (stanzas 1 and 3) and 'the years, the years' (stanzas 2 and 4), one of the poem's many exact symmetries. The 'O' gives the line the ring of a folk-song refrain, as if the speaker could only lament rather than argue. 'Ah, no' is a self-correction: the speaker realises that the scene is past and cannot be held. The refrain is the hinge between two presents, the remembered present of the family and the actual present of decay. It is also the one line in each stanza that does not rhyme.

title: Stanza form
short: Seven-line stanzas: a short-lined scene, the refrain, then a longer final line of decay that rhymes back to line 1.
body: Each stanza rhymes a b c b c, then the unrhymed refrain, then a final line rhyming with the first (songs/throngs, moss/across, all/wall, house/ploughs). Lines 1 to 5 are short and lilting, with the fourth line, like this one, the shortest; the final line is longer and is set further out to the left, so it reads as an outside voice of weather breaking into the song. The return of the first rhyme in the last line encloses the happy scene inside its own ruin. The strict repetition of the pattern is itself expressive: time comes round in each stanza, as the seasons do, and always ends the same way.

title: 'the sick leaves reel down in throngs'
short: Autumn leaves fall like a crowd; 'sick' and 'reel' make them dying, giddy bodies, and 'throngs' answers the gathered family.
body: This is the first of four final lines of natural destruction: falling leaves, storm-birds, a torn-down rose, rain on gravestones. The sequence darkens by degrees, ending at the grave itself. The words are carefully human: leaves are 'sick', they 'reel' as if drunk or faint, and they come in 'throngs', a crowd that grimly mirrors the family gathered round the singers. The exclamation ('How the sick leaves reel') belongs to the speaker's own moment, set against the remembered scene.

title: creeping moss
short: The family clears moss from the garden paths; moss also foreshadows the neglected graves of the last stanza.
body: In the scene the household tidies the garden, scraping off moss to make 'the pathways neat'. 'Creeping' gives the moss the slow persistence of time, which the family can clear only for a season. Moss is a traditional sign of age and of untended graves, and the stanza's building and neatening will be undone by the end of the poem, when the carved names are left to the rain. 'Gay' (l. 11) has its older sense of bright and cheerful.

title: shady seat
short: A garden bench or arbour built for leisure; it is the last thing the family makes before the refrain breaks in.
body: The family builds a shady seat for future summers, an act of confidence in time to come. The phrase looks forward to the 'summer tree' of the next stanza and to a future the speaker knows did not last. Like the other domestic details, it gives the reader the sense of an ordinary, secure Victorian middle-class home, which makes the interruption of the refrain all the more abrupt.

title: storm-birds
short: Sea-birds, gulls or petrels, that fly inland before bad weather and so foretell a storm.
body: A 'storm-bird' is a bird whose appearance is thought to forecast storm; the OED applies the term especially to the petrel. The sea-bird image sits easily with the coastal setting suggested by 'the bay' in the next stanza. In the poem's sequence of final lines they are omens, the weather of time arriving over the garden the family has just made neat. The command 'See' pulls the reader into the speaker's present moment.

title: blithely breakfasting
short: A summer breakfast out of doors; 'blithely' (gladly, carelessly) stresses the family's unawareness of time.
body: 'Blithe' is an old word for joyful and light-hearted, now mainly literary. The scene of breakfast under a tree, with 'pet fowl' coming up to the knee, is the most relaxed of the four, the high summer of the household's happiness. The alliteration (blithely, breakfasting) and the pairing 'Men and maidens' keep the song-like lilt of the earlier stanzas, so that this is the scene the refrain interrupts most cruelly.

title: the bay
short: Probably Plymouth Sound, seen from the Gifford family home in Emma's girlhood.
body: Emma Gifford was born in Plymouth in 1840 and grew up there; around 1860, when the family's finances declined, they moved to a cheaper house near Bodmin in Cornwall. The 'glimpse of the bay' places the scene by the sea, which ties it to Plymouth and to the sea-birds of the previous stanza. The detail is small but exact, and may well be a remembered particular from Emma's account of her childhood, though the poem does not name the place.

anchor: pet fowl come to the knee
title: pet fowl
short: Tame hens or doves that come up to be fed, a detail of easy domestic comfort.
body: The tame birds coming to the diners' knees contrast with the wild 'white storm-birds' of the previous stanza: one is a sign of a safe, enclosed home, the other of weather and the open sea. The phrase shows how precisely Hardy fills each scene with particular, almost photographic detail, as though he were looking at an old family picture, and the fowl, like the family, belong to a vanished moment.

title: 'the rotten rose is ript from the wall'
short: The climbing rose, traditional emblem of beauty and youth, is torn from the wall by the wind; 'ript' is an old spelling of 'ripped'.
body: The rose has long stood for brief beauty in English lyric (as in Herrick's 'Gather ye rose-buds while ye may'). Here it is already 'rotten' before the wind tears it down. The harsh alliteration of r-sounds (rotten, rose, ript) makes this the most violent of the poem's final lines, and 'ript', an older form of the past participle, gives it a hard, abrupt sound. The passive voice leaves the agent unnamed: it is the wind, or time itself.

title: 'a high new house'
short: Literally a move to a larger home; some readers also hear an ironic hint of heaven or of the grave.
body: On the literal level the family moves house and sets out its furniture on the lawn, a scene that readers sometimes connect with the Giffords' changes of home. Some readers take 'high new house' as an image of death, either a heavenly mansion (compare John 14:2, 'In my Father's house are many mansions') or the narrow 'house' of the grave. Others object that Hardy, who did not hold an orthodox faith, would hardly offer a consoling image of heaven, and that the irony lies rather in the gap between the family's pride in its new house and the gravestones of the last line. The poem keeps both senses open.

title: Clocks and carpets and chairs
short: The household goods set out on the lawn during the move; the clocks quietly bring time into the scene.
body: The furniture is carried out 'On the lawn all day', the odd, exposed moment of a house removal. The catalogue repeats the pattern of the earlier lists of people (He, she; Elders and juniors; Men and maidens), so that persons are now replaced by possessions, and 'brightest things that are theirs' are what remain. The first item is 'Clocks': the instruments that measure the years lead the procession.

title: 'Down their carved names the rain-drop ploughs'
short: The final image: rain runs down the family's names cut in gravestones, wearing them as a plough furrows earth.
body: The poem is usually read as ending where all its scenes were heading, at the graves, since the 'carved names' suggest gravestones. The single rain-drop 'ploughs' down the carved letters: a tiny force that, repeated over years, erodes stone, as the refrain's 'years' erode the family. 'Ploughs' turns the gravestone into a field furrowed by time, and the line rhymes back to 'house' in the stanza's first line, binding the new house to the grave. The present tense places the speaker, and the reader, in the rain now, after all the people are dead.
